toc.title: Training, adaptation methods, data preparation and practice

html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Describe the key elements of training a foundation model: pre-training, fine-tuning, continued pre-training and distillation
  • Define the methods for fine-tuning: instruction tuning, domain adaptation and transfer learning
  • Describe how to prepare data: curation, governance, size, labeling, representativeness and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)

2Training, adaptation methods, data preparation and practice

Running case

Cedar and Salt Considers Training

  • Prompts and RAG help, but the team wants the model to write in Cedar and Salt's own style
  • They hold thousands of labeled review summaries and many internal manuals
  • Chat is costly on a large model, and some data holds guest details
  • Your job: choose the method and prepare the data the right way

Training a Foundation Model: The Key Elements

  • Pre-training: a model learns from a broad body of unlabeled data, using self-supervised learning that creates labels from the input itself
  • Building one from scratch can cost millions of dollars, so most teams start from a pre-trained model
  • Adaptation then makes it fit your needs: fine-tuning, continued pre-training and distillation
  • Common training settings: epochs (passes through the data), learning rate (how fast the weights change) and batch size
  • Training in Amazon Bedrock is billed on tokens processed times epochs, plus storage

Exam tip: Pre-training learns general language from unlabeled data; adaptation makes it fit.

The Ways to Adapt a Pre-Trained Model

  • Fine-tuning: labeled prompt and response pairs for a specific task
  • Continued pre-training: unlabeled text from your domain
  • Distillation: a smaller student learns from a larger teacher
  • RLHF: human rankings steer the model toward preferred answers
  • Fine-tuning and continued pre-training change the weights

Exam tip: The type of data decides the method: labeled, unlabeled, teacher output or human ranking.

Fine-Tuning and Instruction Tuning

  • Fine-tuning trains a pre-trained model further, to improve performance on specific tasks
  • Instruction tuning uses labeled examples formatted as prompt and response pairs, phrased as instructions
  • It changes the model's weights
  • Use it when prompt engineering is not enough: business-specific needs, domain jargon and better task results
  • Fine-tuned models such as FLAN-T5 become better at zero-shot tasks, and can be tuned further
  • It needs labeled data

Exam tip: Labeled prompt and response pairs for one task: fine-tuning, or instruction tuning.

Domain Adaptation and Continued Pre-Training [Verify live]

  • Domain adaptation adapts a pre-trained model to domain-specific language, such as industry jargon and technical terms
  • It uses plain, unlabeled text from the domain, such as reports and manuals
  • Continued pre-training in Amazon Bedrock also uses unlabeled data, to make a model more domain-specific
  • Both modify the weights and need no labels
  • As of 5 November 2026: the Amazon Bedrock customization page lists supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement fine-tuning and distillation; check which methods your model supports

Exam tip: Unlabeled domain text to learn vocabulary: domain adaptation, or continued pre-training.

Transfer Learning and Distillation

Method What happens Benefit
Transfer learning A model pre-trained on one task is fine-tuned for a new, related task Faster, with less data and compute
Distillation A larger teacher passes knowledge to a smaller, faster student A cheaper, quicker model for your use case
  • In Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation, teacher responses come from your prompts or from invocation logs, and they fine-tune the student
  • Teacher calls can add on-demand charges; only you can access the distilled model

Exam tip: Reuse a pre-trained model for a new task: transfer learning. Smaller and cheaper: distillation.

Preparing Data to Fine-Tune

Concern What to do
Data curation Select relevant, accurate examples; remove errors and duplicates
Governance Confirm you may use the data; protect personal information; control access
Size Enough examples for the task; limits vary by model; hold out a validation set
Labeling Pair each prompt with a correct, consistent response
Representativeness Cover the real mix of tasks, languages and users, to avoid bias

Exam tip: Quality, governance and coverage beat raw volume.

Fine-Tuning Data in Practice

  • Amazon Bedrock takes training data as JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Lines (.jsonl) files: one record per line
  • A training dataset is required; a validation dataset is optional for many models
  • Text tasks use a prompt and a completion field; chat models use system, user and assistant messages
  • Store the files in Amazon S3; plan size at about six characters per token
  • Your inputs and customizations stay private to your AWS account and are not shared with model providers

Exam tip: Fine-tuning data is labeled, in prompt and completion form, and kept private.

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)

  • RLHF uses human feedback to align a model with human preferences
  • 1. Collect data: people write prompts and good responses
  • 2. Fine-tune a pre-trained model on those pairs
  • 3. Build a reward model: people rank several responses, and the rankings train a reward model
  • 4. Optimize: the model uses the reward model to favor higher-rated answers
  • It helps with qualities hard to measure, such as helpful, harmless and friendly

Exam tip: Humans rank answers to train a reward model: RLHF.

Which Method for Which Data?

You have Use
Labeled prompt and response pairs for one task Fine-tuning (instruction tuning)
Unlabeled text from your domain Domain adaptation or continued pre-training
A large teacher model and a need for a cheaper one Distillation
Human rankings of answers RLHF
A pre-trained model and a new, related task Transfer learning
Vast unlabeled data and large budgets Pre-training

Exam tip: Look at the data first, then name the method.

What the Exam Asks: Training and Fine-Tuning

  • Which element: pre-training, fine-tuning, continued pre-training or distillation
  • Which method: instruction tuning, domain adaptation or transfer learning
  • Which data: labeled for fine-tuning, unlabeled for continued pre-training
  • Which preparation step: curation, governance, size, labeling or representativeness
  • Which technique uses people: RLHF

Exam tip: Name the data first, then the method.

Design Check: Cedar and Salt's Training Plan

What the team has Name and answer
Thousands of labeled review summaries Fine-tuning (instruction tuning)
Many internal manuals, no labels Domain adaptation or continued pre-training
Chat costs too much on a large model Distillation to a smaller student
Replies must feel friendly, rated by staff RLHF
Training data holds guest names and emails Governance: remove or protect personal data
Examples are only in English, guests are global Representativeness: add other languages
  • Cover the right column, answer each row yourself, then compare

3Exam Q&A

3.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1Which description fits the pre-training of a foundation model?

  • ATraining on a small labeled set of prompts for one task
  • BTraining on a broad body of unlabeled data for general ability
  • CTraining a small student model from a larger teacher model
  • DTraining a reward model from rankings made by people
Show the answer

Answer: B. Pre-training uses a broad body of generalized, unlabeled data and self-supervised learning. The other options describe fine-tuning, distillation and RLHF.

S2Cedar and Salt holds 2,000 labeled examples of ideal review summaries. Which approach best improves the model on this one task?

  • ADistillation into a much smaller student model
  • BContinued pre-training on unlabeled brochure text
  • CFine-tuning with labeled prompt and response pairs
  • DPre-training a new foundation model from scratch
Show the answer

Answer: C. Fine-tuning, or instruction tuning, uses labeled prompt and response pairs to improve performance on a specific task. Distillation shrinks a model, continued pre-training uses unlabeled text, and pre-training from scratch is the most costly.

S3Which TWO are considerations when preparing data to fine-tune a foundation model? (Select TWO.)

  • AThe data should represent the real tasks and users
  • BMore data is always better, whatever its quality
  • CPersonal data needs governance, such as removal or protection
  • DThe data must be unlabeled for every fine-tuning method
  • EThe data should be copied from public sources unchecked
Show the answer

Answer: A, C. Data should be curated, governed, labeled and representative of real use. Volume without quality does not help, fine-tuning uses labeled data, and unchecked copying risks errors, bias and rights problems.

S4Cedar and Salt wants a smaller, cheaper model to match the quality of a large model on its chat prompts. Which technique fits?

  • AModel distillation, with a large teacher and a small student
  • BContinued pre-training of the large model on the stored chat logs
  • CAdding more training epochs to the large model's current training run
  • DRaising the learning rate so that the large model answers faster
Show the answer

Answer: A. Distillation transfers knowledge from a larger teacher model to a smaller, faster, more cost-efficient student. Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation automates the workflow. The other options do not produce a smaller model.

S5In RLHF, what do human evaluators do?

  • AThey label every single token in the whole pre-training corpus
  • BThey write the source code for the model training job and pipeline
  • CThey choose the temperature setting for each user request live
  • DThey rank responses so a reward model learns preferences
Show the answer

Answer: D. Evaluators rank several responses to the same prompt. The rankings train a reward model, which the language model then uses to favor higher-rated answers.

S6A company wants a model to learn its industry jargon from a large collection of unlabeled manuals. Which method fits best?

  • AInstruction-based fine-tuning with labeled prompt and response pairs
  • BDomain adaptation or continued pre-training on the text
  • CDistillation from a larger teacher model into a smaller student model
  • DRLHF, using rankings of the model's answers made by people
Show the answer

Answer: B. Domain adaptation, or continued pre-training, uses unlabeled domain text to teach vocabulary and context. Instruction tuning needs labeled pairs, distillation needs a teacher, and RLHF needs human rankings.

4Quick Reference Card

  • Training elements: pre-training, fine-tuning, continued pre-training and distillation
  • Methods: instruction tuning, domain adaptation and transfer learning
  • Data decides: labeled for fine-tuning, unlabeled for domain adaptation, human rankings for RLHF
  • Preparation: curation, governance, size, labeling and representativeness
  • Data stays private to your account in Amazon Bedrock
